segments.say: It's New Year's Eve, a little before midnight, and someone called Hanna is sitting on the floor of her living room with a cardboard box in her lap. Hanna isn't a real person. She's someone we've imagined for tonight, so we can follow one familiar feeling from the inside. But you might recognize a lot of it. The fire is low. The street outside is quiet. And the box is full of old diaries.

show.sub: Hanna and a box of diaries

segments.say: Hanna is in her early fifties. She's just written the date for the very last time this year, and a question has crept up on her, the same one that seems to arrive every December. Where did the year go? It feels as if January was only a few weeks ago. The spring, the summer, the long autumn evenings, they all seem to have slipped past while she was looking somewhere else.

So she opens one of the oldest diaries, from a summer when she was about nine years old. And the strange thing is how long that summer feels, even now. There were weeks of it. Bicycle rides, a lake, a long car journey, a grandmother's garden, a thunderstorm she still remembers. In her memory, that single summer seems almost as big as the whole of this last year.

If you've ever felt that, you're in very good company. It may be one of the most common things people say about time. When we're young, the days stretch out like a long road. Later, the years seem to fold up behind us. Many people describe it the same way: as if time itself had started to speed up somewhere along the way, quietly, without asking.

Tonight, we're going to take that feeling seriously. It's real, in the sense that many people experience it. But what's actually going on underneath? Is time really running faster as we get older? Is it a simple trick of arithmetic? Is it something about memory, or attention, or the brain's own sense of rhythm? And is there anything we can do about it, if we'd like the years to feel a little fuller?

Picture the box for a moment. Old notebooks with soft corners. A few with stickers on the covers. Pages full of handwriting that changes as the years go by, from big careful letters to quick, slanting lines. Each notebook holds a year. And yet, when Hanna weighs them in her hands, some years feel enormous, and others feel as if they barely happened at all.

Here's what we'll explore together tonight. The difference between clock time and felt time. What surveys of real people actually show. An old idea about ratios. Busy days, and holidays. Memory as a kind of measuring tape. Novelty and surprise. A famous study where people fell from a tall platform. The body's own clock. Emotion and attention. A strange year in lockdown. And finally, what might help.

We'll go through it a little like a gentle investigation. There are quite a few popular ideas about why time speeds up with age, and some of them are partly right, while others don't hold up very well when scientists test them. So, one by one, we'll take a common belief, look at what research has found, and see what's left standing. No rush. We'll take it slowly.

And then, about two thirds of the way through, we'll let the facts go and turn this into a long, gentle wind-down, so you can drift off whenever you're ready. There's nothing you need to remember tonight. If you fall asleep halfway through a study, that's perfectly fine. The ideas will still be here another night. For now, just get comfortable, and listen.

One small promise before we begin. You don't need any physics tonight, and you won't need to do any sums. Time is a huge subject, and philosophers and physicists have their own deep questions about it. But tonight is about something much closer to home. Not time out there in the universe, but time as it feels from the inside, to an ordinary person sitting on an ordinary floor.

So let's start with the most basic question of all. When Hanna says the year has flown by, what exactly does she mean? Her kitchen clock has ticked at the same pace all year. Every day had the same twenty four hours. Every week had seven days. If you measured this year with a stopwatch, it would be exactly as long as the summer she remembers from when she was nine.

That's the first thing worth noticing. There seem to be two kinds of time in our lives. There's clock time, which is steady and shared, the same for everyone in the room. And there's felt time, which is personal, and stretchy, and changes with our mood, our age and what we're doing. When people say that time speeds up, they're talking about the second kind.

Here's a gentle way to hold that idea. The clock keeps its pace. The feeling does not. That's not a failure of the mind. It's simply how a living brain works. We don't have a perfect stopwatch inside us. Instead, we build our sense of time from many different signals, and those signals can be stretched or squeezed in surprising ways. That's what we'll be exploring tonight.
